source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3600369 (author manuscript of Drug Alcohol Depend 2012;123 Suppl 1:S3-S17), read in full in the reader's own browser tab: Abstract, sections 1-4, funding, contributors, conflict of interest and the whole reference list (get_page_text stopped inside the references; the remaining references were read from the same tab with javascript_tool). Fig. 1 is a conceptual diagram with no data.

claims.overstatement: None. If anything the claim understates the review: besides arguing that the order of first use need not reflect causal steps, the review says the causal reading is readily refuted by atypical sequences, and, citing a book (Earleywine, 2002), that the true cannabis-to-other-drug association is negligible once how common cannabis use is has been taken into account, so it disputes the association itself, not only its causal reading. Precision: 'does not discuss the co-twin evidence' is correct for co-twin-control (discordant-pair) studies; no such study, including Lynskey et al. (2003), is cited anywhere in the text or reference list. The review does rely on classical twin studies of genetic correlation between liabilities (Kendler et al., 2003, 2007; Agrawal et al., 2004), so 'co-twin control studies' would be the exact wording. 'Calls that liability empirically proven' matches the Conclusions, where the concept of common liability is called empirically proven.
claims.note: Narrative review: the Abstract's Method says only that the literature on both concepts is reviewed; no search, selection or appraisal is described, and no new data are presented. Every empirical statement is a citation, many to the authors' own work (the common-liability concept and the transmissible liability index are theirs). The paper opens a journal supplement and its last sentence says the papers in the special issue support its conclusion. Conflicts: none declared; NIDA had no role. Citations relevant to other parts of this claim: (1) it repeats Degenhardt et al. (2010) for Japan (cannabis used by 4.5% and other illegal drugs by 4.8% of people aged 18-29; 83.2% of people who used other illegal drugs had not used cannabis first), which agrees with the claim's 83.2%; (2) it says Morral et al. (2002) showed that the correlations of cannabis with other drug use 'are accounted for' by common liability and opportunity, a stronger reading than a simulation can support, consistent with the claim's own more careful account of Morral. Its arguments that delaying tobacco use does not lower later illegal drug use (Furr-Holden et al., 2004) and that a genetic variant reducing drinking does not predict lower other drug use (Irons et al., 2007) are also second-hand.

anchors.extracted: Method stated only as a review of the literature on the theory and findings for both concepts. The authors conclude that the order of first use is variable and opportunistic, that any association between risks for different drugs is better explained by common underpinnings than by stages, and that common liability is grounded in genetic theory and data.

The authors argue that an association between drugs need not be spurious to be non-causal, and that a common source of risk, together with one drug being more available than another, can explain the order of use; they say causality is refuted by frequent atypical sequences.

Citing a book (Earleywine, 2002), the review says that once the population frequency of cannabis use is taken into account the true cannabis-to-hard-drug association is negligible, and that the high correlations reported are artefacts of estimating them among people who use hard drugs. Second-hand; no data given.

Citing Degenhardt et al. (2010): in Japan cannabis was used by 4.5% and other illegal drugs by 4.8% of people aged 18-29, and 83.2% of people who used other illegal drugs had not used cannabis first; the order and its exceptions follow how common cannabis use is. Also cited: delays in tobacco onset did not lower later cannabis or other illegal drug use (Furr-Holden et al., 2004).

anchors.locator: 3.2.1. Empirical support for the common addiction liability concept, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Support for common liability is drawn from cited work: a statistical simulation said to show that cannabis-other drug correlations are accounted for by common liability and opportunity (Morral et al., 2002); disorder symptoms for different drugs lying on one dimension; and high genetic correlations between liabilities in classical twin studies, with virtually no drug-specific genetic variance apart from a licit/illicit split (Kendler et al., 2003, 2007). No co-twin-control (discordant-pair) study is cited here or elsewhere in the review.

anchors.locator: 3.2.2. Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 7th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The probability of starting with a given drug is said to follow how common its use is and its availability; in the common-liability view the order of first use is not denied but is seen as opportunistic and trivial.

The authors call common liability a parsimonious and empirically proven concept, the gateway hypothesis redundant and of uncertain use, and warn that presenting the sequence as a theory invites causal misreading; they say the special issue's papers support this.
